docstring: A refusal whose rule id declares a thing NOT FOUND / ABSENT / MISSING / `NOT_PRESENT` must carry, in the same refusal, an expression that names WHERE the program looked. LADDER: not Bucket T — upstream has no defect here. librelane declares `PAD_FAKE_SITES` (config/flow.py:494) and materialises it inside `read_tech_lef` (io.tcl:349) BEFORE its own site lookups run (`pad_cfg`.tcl:40), so the sites exist in the DB by the time any padring script asks for them. Ours was the only layer that never opened the declaration; a fork change would paper over our omission. Stop at A. THE EXACT INPUT a program sees: the module's own AST. THE EXACT DECISION from that input: does the call that constructs this refusal contain any expression naming a search locus? That is syntax, not judgement. The one decision it CANNOT make from that input is whether the named search space is COMPLETE — completeness is a property of the DISTRIBUTION, not of our source, and no amount of reading our Python decides whether the two views a PDK declares a site in were both opened. The rule is therefore scoped to the reachable half: refuse an absence verdict that names NO search space at all.
fix_action: THE RULE, CORRECTED TWICE BY MEASUREMENT. Attempt 1 (the prior lane's, shipped nowhere): the message mentions a word from a locus vocabulary -- PASSES the real pre-fix refusal. Attempt 2 (my probe, evidence/`F1_rule_population_probe`.py, not shipped): the message interpolates a name the enclosing function iterated -- refuses 15 of 24, and the first two I read are model disclosures that name their exact path. Both are measuring something ADJACENT to the question and neither error is visible from inside its own implementation. What decides both cases is the thing neither looks at: THE CONDITION THAT RAISED THE REFUSAL. `if not d.is_dir()` -> subject is `d`, message names `d`, complete. `if site is None` -> subject is the lookup that returned None, and the provenance of THAT is what the pre-fix message never disclosed. So the rule is: AN ABSENCE VERDICT MUST NAME THE SUBJECT OF THE CONDITION THAT RAISED IT -- a dataflow question from the refusal back to its guard. Still deterministic, still Bucket A, and real program work rather than a predicate tweak. NOT ATTEMPTED A THIRD TIME: past this point I would be iterating shapes until one came out green on today's corpus, and a predicate arrived at that way is fitted to the corpus rather than to the rule. GENERAL-CORE TEST: reads refusal construction and control flow; no pad, no PDK literal.
prior_art: `origin/jcapsha/capture-sha256-recovery`: programs/`absence_verdict_names_its_search_space_check`.py (407 lines) + test (210). NOT SHIPPED, and the reason is stronger than the one this record first carried. MEASURED on a written control (evidence/`F1_the_guard_does_not_catch_F1`.md): THE ACTUAL PRE-FIX REFUSAL PASSES IT. The message says `LEF(s)` and `lef` is in the guard's locus vocabulary, so the verdict that blocked one design's whole verdict is accepted. The guard is named `names_its_search_space` and decides `mentions_a_locus_word`; the distance between those two predicates IS the defect. On top of that it reports 2 false positives on current main (rc 1) whose messages both DO say where they looked, in vocabulary the 57-word list does not contain. Too lax where it matters and too strict where it does not, and narrowing the word list fixes neither, because the word list is not the part that is wrong. A SECOND HOLE WAS FOUND AND CUT DOWN TO ITS MEASURED SIZE: a verdict reading `f"{name} is not available"` passes solely because bare `name` is in the vocabulary -- a word for the thing SOUGHT, not the place SEARCHED. Real on a constructed input; on main's 1279 files, dropping it changes nothing (31/29/2 either way), so it is latent, not active. Reported at the size the corpus supports, not the size the mechanism suggested.
status: NOT SHIPPED on this branch, and the reason is two independent measurements, not one. The prior lane's implementation PASSES the actual pre-fix refusal (it mentions `LEF(s)`, and `lef` is in its locus vocabulary) while reporting 2 false positives on main. My own implementation of the corrected rule refuses 15 of 24, and the first two I read name their exact path. The rule stands and is Bucket A; what decides it is the condition that RAISED the refusal, which neither implementation looks at. No third predicate was attempted, because past that point it would be fitted to the corpus.

docstring: Where this plugin RE-IMPLEMENTS an upstream computation or configuration contract, a register must account for every upstream name in exactly one class — implemented, `declared_unperformed`, `omitted_by_design` (with a reason), or `known_gap` (with a reason AND a reference) — and a `known_gap` name that DOES appear in our module is a finding, not a pass. LADDER: not Bucket T — upstream's `pad_cfg`.tcl is CORRECT. It measures a cell in exactly two places and both read [[$inst `getMaster`] `getWidth`], on all four sides; there is no `getHeight` in its side arithmetic at all. The 4.4x error (19 x 350 = 6650 um summed against a 1500 um side) was entirely ours, from taking the extent off the ORIENTED footprint. Nothing to fix in a fork. Stop at A. THE EXACT INPUT: the register plus our module's source. THE EXACT DECISION: is every extracted upstream name in exactly one class, and does each class's claim hold against the source? Set arithmetic. The judgement — which class a name belongs in — is made ONCE by a human at registration and then pinned; that is what makes it a ratchet rather than a re-derivation.
fix_action: Register {upstream artefact, `extract_regex`, snapshot of extracted names + file sha256, our module, classification}. Refuse any name not accounted for. CRITICAL PREDICATE FIX, measured: the existing implementation's _mentions() requires the name as a BARE QUOTED LITERAL, so it cannot see a name consumed through a regex — which is exactly how _pad_ring.py:490 consumes `PAD_FAKE_SITES`. Consequence measured on origin/main a4caccefe: the register still classifies `PAD_FAKE_SITES` as `known_gap` while the fix that closed that gap is on main (`parse_pad_site_declarations` :497, `discover_io_site_declarations` :550, `IoLibrary`.`resolve_site` :642), the guard's own staleness rule at :213 exists for precisely this, and it does not fire. The guard exits 0. That PASS is partly blind. GENERAL-CORE TEST: this is F1's class one level up — F1 read one PDK VIEW and said 'not found'; this reads one SOURCE FORM and says 'not implemented'. Both are a search space narrower than the claim made over it.
prior_art: THREE near-duplicate implementations exist across my own prior lanes, none landed: `upstream_reimplementation_pin_check`.py (`UPSTREAM_PINS`, origin/agent/jcapsha-capture), `upstream_mirror_is_pinned_check`.py (`UPSTREAM_MIRROR`, origin/jcapsha/capture-`sha256-recovery`), `upstream_contract_parity_check`.py + register (origin/jcapsha/`sha256-capture`). Measured on current main: the first two exit 2 NOT DETERMINED over a population of ZERO declarations — a green over nothing, not a clean answer. Only the third has a non-vacuous population (20 upstream names, 8 implemented, 3 `declared_unperformed`, 8 `omitted_by_design`, 1 `known_gap`) and it is the one to keep. The deliverable here is a consolidation verdict and a predicate fix, NOT a fourth checker.
routing_note: Routed to its own repo-level step. The first version of this branch registered this route while deliberately NOT shipping the program, and `test_capture_routing_consistency.py` failed on the dangling path. The route is restored here because the program is now shipped and green, not because the gate was talked round.
status: SHIPPED on this branch and green: `upstream_contract_parity_check.py`, its register (THREE entries now, one of them with no pad in it), and two pin test files. Zero open gaps -- `known_gap=0` on the contract entry and both computation entries at `pin=test`. Reds behind it: reverting the predicate; silencing the unclassified-name loop; silencing the excuse-list finding; upstream dropping `read_def` from its default route; our producer dropping `def read`; upstream summing the height instead of the width; a pin naming a test that was never written; and the sha-guard disabled. Every mutation asserts that the property actually changed before it reports.

docstring: A configuration variable that a step DECLARES in its contract but does not implement must degrade loudly: at the upstream default (indistinguishable from never having set it) PROCEED and record the non-honouring in EVERY report including the skips, because a disclosure only on the happy path is not a disclosure; DELIBERATELY SET to a non-default, refuse rc=2 NOT DETERMINED naming the variable — never rc 0, never rc 1, because 'I cannot honour what you asked' is neither a pass nor a finding about the design. LADDER — AND THE BRIEF'S PREMISE FOR THIS ONE IS REFUTED. The brief states `PAD_ROTATION_VERTICAL` was 'proven inert by four separate OpenROAD processes'. It is NOT inert, and the source that proves it is the report I was sent to capture: re-measured in OpenROAD 26Q3-1581 holding one rotation parameter and varying the other across ALL FOUR sides, -`rotation_horizontal` moves WEST and EAST and -`rotation_vertical` moves SOUTH and NORTH. THE PARAMETERS ARE NAMED FOR THE ROW AXIS, NOT THE SIDE. The original probe varied `PAD_ROTATION_VERTICAL` while observing only WEST and EAST — the wrong pairing — so it correctly saw no change and the wrong conclusion was drawn from a correct measurement. WHICH HALF IS WHICH, as the brief asks: there is no tool half. The tool honours the variable and is self-consistent with its own naming convention; renaming a fork's CLI flags to match a side-based reading would break every upstream script that drives it. The whole of this finding is ours. Bucket T is empty for a MEASURED reason, not a judgement call. Stop at A. THE EXACT INPUT: the step's declared config contract plus the variable's resolved value. THE EXACT DECISION: is this name in the not-honoured set, and is its value non-default? A lookup and a comparison.
fix_action: Keep a not-honoured set beside the contract. On a non-default value for any member, exit 2 NOT DETERMINED naming the variable. On the default, proceed and emit the disclosure into every report the step writes, skips included. THE SCHEMA KEY MUST NOT ASSERT THE REFUTED PREMISE: the shipped record keyed this `rotation_vertical_inert`, which asserts inertness in the schema itself; it is `rotation_vertical_not_honoured` (fixed in c56b8e1b1). The ruling's BEHAVIOUR is unchanged by the refutation and its justification gets stronger — the weak version was 'an author who sets a knob is entitled to be told it does nothing'; the true one is that the knob HAS an effect, it rotates the N/S pads, and this step does not implement it, so honouring the declaration silently would hand an author geometry they did not ask for. GENERAL-CORE TEST: generalise the RULE, not the variable — the logic reads a contract and a value, and knows nothing about pads or rotation.
prior_art: The second recovery inside this one is a probe lesson and it is F1's class again, a third time: a NEGATIVE result is only evidence if the probe could have observed a positive. Four separate processes were run — the process-isolation confound was correctly removed — and the observation space was still one side-pair out of two. Folded here rather than emitted as a fourth rule because 'an assertion of a negative must name what it observed' is the same rule as 'an absence verdict must name what it searched', and the brief's warning about near-duplicate checkers applies to my own records too.
status: RULE CAPTURED, no code change needed on this branch: the ruling's BEHAVIOUR is already on main -- a non-default value is refused rc 2 NOT DETERMINED naming the variable. What is not on main is the corrected justification, which is the next record.

docstring: A finding recorded in a SCHEMA KEY, a CONSTANT NAME or a REPORT FIELD cannot be retracted by prose elsewhere. When the finding is refuted, the identifier changes in the same commit that records the refutation, because every downstream reader keys on the identifier and none of them reads the retraction. LADDER: not Bucket T (no tool is involved in what we name our own fields), not B or C (nothing here needs judgement). THE EXACT INPUT: the shipped source plus the record of what was refuted. THE EXACT DECISION: does an identifier still assert a proposition the project has recorded as false? That is a comparison between two written-down things. MEASURED ON `origin/main` `a4caccefe`, and this is a LIVE state, not a historical one: the report that refutes the inertness premise says the rename landed in `c56b8e1b1`. `git merge-base --is-ancestor c56b8e1b1 origin/main` says it is NOT an ancestor. Main today ships the artefact key `rotation_vertical_inert` (`pad_ring_gen.py`:246), the constant `ROTATION_VERTICAL_INERT` with `honoured`: False (:185), the section heading that the variable IS INERT (:67), and the comment that the placer does not read it. Every one of those asserts, in the schema and in the source, the proposition the branch's own re-measurement withdrew.
fix_action: Rename the key and the constant to `rotation_vertical_not_honoured` / `ROTATION_VERTICAL_NOT_HONOURED` and restate the two comments as what was actually measured: the variable is not inert, it steers the SOUTH and NORTH rows, and THIS STEP does not implement it. The behaviour of the ruling does not change and its justification gets stronger. AND A SECOND CONSEQUENCE, NAMED BUT NOT CONFIRMED BY ME, because I have run no tool: if the re-measured table is right that `rotation_horizontal` steers WEST and EAST while `rotation_vertical` steers SOUTH and NORTH, then main's side map is TRANSPOSED -- `pad_ring_gen.py`:317-318 drives SOUTH and NORTH from `PAD_ROTATION_HORIZONTAL`, and WEST and EAST come from the hard-coded `VERTICAL_SIDE_ORIENT` constants, which were measured only at that variable's default. A design declaring a non-default `PAD_ROTATION_HORIZONTAL` would then get emitted orientations the placer does not produce, and the rc=2 refusal guards the OTHER variable, so nothing stops it. THIS NEEDS ONE OPENROAD RUN TO SETTLE AND MUST NOT BE ACTED ON UNTIL IT HAS ONE. It is written down because an unverified consequence that is named can be checked, and one that is not named cannot.
prior_art: `origin/jcapsha/sha256-capture` carries a Bucket B candidate on the same axis vocabulary, and `origin/jpadsite/capture-bundle` carries the commit that first caught the probe error. Neither landed, and the identifier is still on main, which is the point of this record: the refutation was published four times across four branches and the shipped key never changed.
evidence: RESULT.md section: main still ships the refuted premise
status: SHIPPED on this branch. I declined this once with 'the fix is a rename on main and the brief forbids pushing to main' -- which conflates two things: every fix here reaches main THROUGH A BRANCH, which is how the checker shipped. I had over-restricted myself and left a measured, bounded defect in place on that basis. CHANGED: the artefact key, the constant, the heading, four prose claims, the user-visible rc 2 reason, two TEST NAMES and one local variable -- a test name is an identifier and asserts the same proposition a schema key does. NOT CHANGED: any geometry, orientation value or verdict; the finding rule id was already correct and the mutation asserts it survives, so a careless global rename cannot pass as this fix. Two new tests, one of them the GENERAL rule walked over the producer's AST. Mutation: every spelling reverted, rule id spared -> 4 failed, 95 passed; restored -> 99 passed, byte-identical. The transposition question stays OPEN in the comment where a reader meets it: it needs one OpenROAD run and I have run no tool.
